query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small reactive element, such as yttrium, to the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will enable the in situ formation of a continuous, lubricious oxide tribolayer at elevated temperatures, thereby maintaining a low friction coefficient and wear rate from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix without additional reactive dopants.
generation.intervention: Doping the alloy with a minor concentration (e.g., 0.5–1 wt%) of a reactive element (yttrium) during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: Sliding contact experiments conducted in air under controlled load and speed, over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a thin, stable Y-rich oxide tribolayer on the wear surface during sliding.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the alloy behaves similarly to the baseline. At elevated temperatures, the added yttrium oxidizes preferentially to form a adherent, lubricious oxide layer that prevents direct metal-to-metal contact, limiting abrasive wear and reducing friction.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped CoCrFeNi alloy, the Y-doped alloy is expected to exhibit consistently lower friction coefficients and wear rates across the entire temperature range.
generation.baseline: Sliding performance (friction coefficient and wear rate) of the undoped CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy.
generation.boundary: This behavior is anticipated under moderate to high loads in an air environment where oxidation can occur, specifically within the temperature range from ambient to 800 °C.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal concentration of yttrium and the kinetics of oxide tribolayer formation may vary with sliding conditions and environmental factors, potentially affecting the magnitude of friction and wear reduction.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy samples: one baseline (undoped) and one doped with 0.5–1 wt% yttrium. Conduct standardized pin-on-disk sliding tests across a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under identical loads, sliding speeds, and environmental (air) conditions.
measurements: Coefficient of friction recorded continuously during sliding tests
Wear rate measured post-test by quantifying material loss
Surface analysis (e.g., XPS, SEM) to verify formation and continuity of the Y-rich oxide tribolayer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped samples do not show a statistically significant decrease in friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the undoped samples across the entire temperature range, or if no continuous Y-rich oxide layer is detectable on the wear surface at elevated temperatures, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In this study, the wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy coating was systematically analyzed by the molecular dynamics method. FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy was used as a coating material to adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix. The friction and nanoindentation simulation of this coating material were carried out by controlling the ambient temperature. The influence of temperature on its friction properties was analyzed on five aspects: lattice structure, dislocation evolution, friction coefficient, hardness, and elastic modulus. The results show that with the increase of temperature, the disorder of the lattice structure increases, which leads to an increase of the tangential force and friction coefficient in the friction process. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] .
